text: The 1906 Bodmin by-election was held on 24 July 1906 for the British House of Commons constituency of Bodmin in Cornwall. It was triggered by the unseating of the Liberal Member of Parliament Thomas Agar-Robartes due to an election petition alleging illegal payments to potential voters. The petition's success was controversial because the presiding judge, Justice Grantham—a former Conservative MP—had previously faced criticism for a decision in the Great Yarmouth constituency that was seen as unduly favourable to the Conservatives. A censure motion against Grantham was pending in Parliament at the time, but the Government chose not to pursue it. Five years later, Grantham was censured by Prime Minister H. H. Asquith for comments made to a jury in a Liverpool case. The Liberal candidate in the by-election was Freeman Freeman-Thomas, who had lost his seat in Hastings in the recent general election. The Liberal Unionist candidate was George Sandys. Agar-Robartes' brother toured the constituency, urging voters to support the Liberal cause in response to the petition's outcome. The Unionists claimed the Government intended to make up to 20,000 soldiers unemployed, a claim denied by Secretary of War Richard Haldane. Freeman-Thomas won the by-election with a slightly reduced majority—dropping from 1,172 to 1,093—on a turnout that was somewhat smaller than in the general election. George Sandys later served as Conservative MP for Wells from 1910 to 1918, and his son, Duncan Sandys, became an MP and cabinet minister.
